course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: Labor, Slavery, and Caste in the Spanish Colonial System
lesson.summary: How the encomienda, African slavery, and the casta system organized work and social rank across the Spanish empire in the Americas.
learningGoals: Explain how the encomienda system used Native American labor in mining and agriculture.
Explain why enslaved Africans were brought to the Spanish colonies and how Europeans obtained them.
Describe the casta system and how it ranked the people of the Spanish empire.
lesson.bigIdea: Spanish colonial economies were built on forced labor, first from Native Americans and then from enslaved Africans, and a rigid caste system ranked people by ancestry.
lesson.context: The CED asks how the growth of the Spanish empire shaped social and economic structures over time. Think about how labor, wealth, and rank connected.

sections.title: The encomienda and Native labor

blocks.text: Spanish rulers rewarded conquistadors and settlers with grants called encomiendas. An encomienda gave a colonist the right to demand labor and tribute from a Native community. In return, the holder was supposed to protect the people and teach them Christianity, but in practice the system often meant brutal work and heavy losses of life.

Native workers mined silver, grew sugar and other crops, and herded livestock. In the Andes, Spanish officials adapted an Inca labor draft called the mita to supply workers for the silver mines at Potosí. Spain used Native labor to extract precious metals and to support plantation agriculture across its empire.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: The encomienda was not slavery in law, because the Crown claimed Native peoples were its free subjects. In practice, forced and unpaid labor often looked much like slavery.

sections.takeaway: The encomienda gave Spanish colonists control over Native labor and tribute, which fueled mining and plantation agriculture.

sections.title: Enslaved Africans in the Spanish and Portuguese Americas
sections.conceptTitle: Enslaved Africans in the Spanish and Portuguese Americas

blocks.text: Slavery already existed in Africa, the Mediterranean, and Europe, and Portuguese traders had been buying enslaved Africans since the 1400s. Along the African coast, Europeans partnered with some West African groups that practiced slavery. These partners captured people and sold them to Europeans, who forcibly transported them across the Atlantic.

The Spanish began importing enslaved Africans to the Caribbean in the early 1500s. Demand grew as epidemics, overwork, and abuse reduced the Native workforce. Enslaved Africans labored on sugar plantations and in mines throughout the Spanish empire, and Portuguese colonists in Brazil built a large plantation economy on enslaved labor.

blocks.title: Cause and effect
blocks.text: Native populations declined, labor shortages followed, and colonists and the Crown turned to enslaved Africans, which expanded the Atlantic slave trade.

sections.takeaway: Labor shortages after Native population decline increased reliance on enslaved Africans obtained through partnerships on the African coast.

sections.title: The casta system

blocks.text: Spanish settlers formed families with Native and African partners, and the empire's population became very mixed. To organize this society, Spanish officials and the Church developed a caste system, known as the casta system, that ranked people by ancestry and color.

At the top were peninsulares, people born in Spain, who held the highest government and Church offices. Below them were criollos, people of Spanish descent born in the Americas. Mestizos had Spanish and Native ancestry, and mulattoes had Spanish and African ancestry. Native Americans paid tribute and provided labor, and enslaved Africans held the lowest position. Rank shaped legal rights, occupations, and taxes, though some people could improve their standing.

sections.takeaway: The casta system defined each group's status by ancestry and tied social rank to rights, work, and taxes.

connections.title: Labor, ideas, and resistance
connections.body: Forced labor and rank created conflict and debate. Topic 1.6 follows how Native peoples resisted and how Europeans argued about how Native peoples and Africans should be treated.
connections.transferQuestion: How did the casta system reflect the economic goals of the Spanish empire?
connections.feedback: A strong answer links rank to access to land, office, and labor, and explains how the empire's wealth depended on keeping some groups at the bottom.
